authors: M. J. P. Perkasa, H. M. Ramdan, A. J. Maliki, and Somantri
title: Implementation of Secure End-to-End Encrypted Chat Application Using Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange and AES-256 in a Microservice Architecture
venue: Engineering Proceedings (MDPI), Proc. 7th International Global Conference Series on ICT Integration in Technical Education & Smart Society (ICTI 2025)
one_line: A working secure end-to-end encrypted chat application combining ECDH/Diffie-Hellman key exchange and AES-256 (CBC) within a scalable microservice backend, validated through functional tests and an AES throughput benchmark.
problem: Securely exchanging encryption keys in client-server/REST architectures can expose weaknesses that enable unauthorized access, and chat applications struggle with scalability and maintainability as traffic grows. The authors aim to build a chat system that guarantees message confidentiality from sender to recipient (no intermediary, including the server, can decrypt) while remaining scalable and modular.
methods: The system uses Diffie-Hellman / Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH, via the Web Crypto API) to derive an identical shared secret on each client without ever transmitting private keys, then encrypts messages with AES-256 in CBC mode before transmission; RSA is also referenced for asymmetric/small-data use. The backend is a microservice architecture: NGINX API Gateway (routing, WebSocket upgrade, load balancing/reverse proxy), Authentication Service (port 8081, credential verification, JWT issuance), WebSocket Service (8082, real-time bi-directional message routing), Chat Service (8083/8084, message storage and conversation management with horizontal scaling), PostgreSQL (5432, stores encrypted messages and auth data), and RabbitMQ (5672, asynchronous inter-service messaging). Authentication uses phone-number plus SMS verification code then JWT; flows for user creation/key generation, conversation creation/key exchange, and send/receive are described. Evaluation is functional testing of each stage (showing messages stored encrypted in the DB and decrypted only by holders of the shared key) plus an AES encrypt/decrypt benchmark over varying message counts (10; 100; 1000; 10,000; 100,000) using the test string 'Hello, secure world!'.
key_findings: Diffie-Hellman/ECDH key exchange produced an identical, real-time shared key on both client sides without transmitting any private key; the server only ever sees the public keys.

Messages are encrypted (AES-256 CBC) on the client before transmission and are stored encrypted in PostgreSQL, so only the sender and recipient holding the identical shared key can decrypt them, achieving end-to-end confidentiality even against a compromised server.

The microservice architecture (API Gateway, Auth, WebSocket, Chat, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ) supports scalability, modularity, and reduced single points of failure, with horizontal scaling of the Chat Service across multiple ports.

Functional tests confirmed the full pipeline (account creation, JWT auth, ECDH key generation, conversation/key exchange, encrypted send/receive and successful decryption) works with low latency and high throughput, per the authors' qualitative claims.
An AES encryption/decryption benchmark was run across message counts of 10 to 100,000 to characterize performance (results shown only as a figure).
metrics: Diffie-Hellman illustrative example: prime P=23, primitive root g=5, Alice private a=3 (public A=10), Bob private b=7 (public B=17), shared key=14
ECDH key strength claim: 256-bit ECDH key ~ equivalent security to 3072-bit classic Diffie-Hellman
AES: 128-bit block; key lengths 128/192/256 bits; rounds Nr = 10/12/14 respectively
AES benchmark message counts tested: 10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000 (timing results presented only in Figure 26, no numeric values given in text)
Sample server request latencies from logs: PUT /users 13.5 ms; POST /conversations ~59.7 ms
strengths: Concrete, implemented end-to-end system (not just a design) with real test logs, JWT tokens, ECDH keys, and encrypted DB records demonstrating that the server cannot read message content.
Clear separation of concerns via microservices (gateway, auth, websocket, chat, broker, database) giving practical scalability, modularity, and fault tolerance guidance.
Uses standard, well-vetted primitives (ECDH via Web Crypto API, AES-256-CBC, JWT) and documents the full key-exchange and messaging flow step by step.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is thin: the AES benchmark results are shown only as a figure with no reported numbers, and 'low latency/high throughput' claims are not backed by stated metrics.

AES-CBC is used without explicit mention of authenticated encryption (e.g., HMAC/GCM), leaving integrity/tampering protection unclear; ECDH lacks an authentication mechanism, so man-in-the-middle resistance depends on out-of-band trust (the paper itself notes ECDH's MITM weakness).

Authentication relies on phone-number plus SMS code and server-stored credentials, which is susceptible to SIM-swap/interception and is not privacy-preserving; no formal security analysis or threat model is provided.
The literature-review section is loosely written and partly repetitive, and the inconsistent references to RSA, DH, and ECDH make the exact deployed key-exchange scheme slightly ambiguous.
relevance: This paper directly underpins SentriZK's third pillar (end-to-end encrypted transport via Diffie-Hellman/ECDH key exchange plus AES-256) and demonstrates a concrete microservice backend (API gateway, WebSocket service, message broker, encrypted-at-rest storage) of the kind SentriZK's enterprise messaging server can adopt. It also highlights gaps SentriZK aims to close: its ECDH lacks authentication and MITM protection (which SentriZK addresses with zero-knowledge-proof authentication instead of fragile manual ceremonies), and it has no on-device threat detection (SentriZK's second pillar).
ieee_reference: M. J. P. Perkasa, H. M. Ramdan, A. J. Maliki, and Somantri, "Implementation of secure end-to-end encrypted chat application using Diffie-Hellman key exchange and AES-256 in a microservice architecture," Eng. Proc., vol. 107, no. 1, art. 98, 2025, doi: 10.3390/engproc2025107098.
